RELEASE therefore deletes the frames' standing caveat ('release untested') WITHOUT changing what the acceptance measures: a strict option with no cost in substance, the price being only a cold build's time. And his third point inverts my own counter-argument: if RELEASE ever diverges from DEBUG, that is a finding to obtain BEFORE the acceptance rather than something hidden by picking the profile that matches the pictures - exact agreement with what was expected proves almost nothing while feeling like proof.
what_I_can_and_cannot_verify_about_the_e:
This replaces the manager's STOP as he wrote it, by his own instruction, because his version named a measurement that does not exist. THE INPUT is verifiable with certainty: `tauri.conf.json` declares `build.frontendDist = ../dist`, so the build reads that directory, and the driver pins dist/index.html to 96b6bd5000f957155569b342a236c17b51e244a8291475cf82260d1980fdf3fa both BEFORE and AFTER, since a build must not rewrite its own input. THE OUTPUT is NOT verifiable by inspecting the binary, and that is measured rather than assumed.

How it was measured, including the part where I was briefly fooled: I searched the existing 2026-09-30 release binary for one of the NEW texts and got 0, which agreed with expectation ('an old binary has no new strings') and would have been banked. The POSITIVE CONTROL destroyed it - a string that MUST be there, `Войдите в аккаунт Skipi`, also returned 0, proving the instrument blind rather than the binary old. Then I measured HOW blind: `strings` finds `<!DOCTYPE html` (5 hits) and `<title>` (4) but NOT `mobile-status`, NOT `loginRefusalText`, NOT `data-theme`, and ZERO Cyrillic anywhere - the 1,131,783-byte document is stored compressed. And no asset manifest with a digest is left under target/release/build/*/out (checked: that tree holds dependency codegen like named_entities.rs and bindgen.rs, nothing about frontend assets).

So the honest chain is: input proven by digest, output provable only by RUNNING the thing - which is the smoke stage, agreed as the next one.
no_network_and_offline_is_what_makes_tha: `ports` is empty, and `--offline` is what earns it rather than hope. The shared registry cache holds 814 .crate files against 595 packages in the lock - but 814 >= 595 is a COUNT, not a composition, and it does not prove the right VERSIONS are present. I am not inferring from it. `--offline` makes cargo answer the question itself: if anything is missing it fails loudly, and that failure is returned as a finding rather than repaired by reaching for the network mid-stage. The registry cache is declared as a READ.
the_window_floor_is_not_a_promise_of_fin: 240 s, which is nearly the whole window, and the reason is unusual: a cold release build of 595 packages will almost certainly OUTLAST any 300 s lease, and no floor can promise otherwise. So the floor does not mean 'enough time to finish' - it means 'start only at the BEGINNING of a window', so that an overrun is unambiguously an overrun rather than a near-miss. Per the standing rule the command is NOT interrupted on expiry: it is carried to the end and the stage closes with ack-stop from DRAIN_REQUIRED. Killing a build mid-flight would leave a partial target and there is no safe boundary inside it. The wall clock is recorded, and `overran_window=yes|no` goes into the record as a fact rather than an apology.
the_positive_control_is_available_here_u: Stage 9 had to switch to a content-based control because stage 5's success had SPENT the 'absent -> exists' transition on FETCH_HEAD. release_sensitive_files_are_guarded_by_a: `Cargo.lock` and `Cargo.toml` are release-sensitive in this house and out of scope for a non-release task - they are exactly what blocked an earlier push. `--locked` makes cargo REFUSE rather than rewrite the lock, and that is a flag, i.e. a promise. So both digests are also compared after the build, and a change is a FINDING plus exit 22, not a note. The same treatment for dist/index.html: a build must not rewrite its own input.
a_blind_spot_in_check_undefined_funcs_re:
My first draft used `command -v cargo`, and the checker reported `command` as an undefined function: it reads a shell BUILTIN at statement start as a call. Isolated with minimal cases: `command -v ls` is flagged as `command`, `type -p ls` as `type`, while `export X=1` and `eval "f"` stay clean - so it is builtins MISSING FROM ITS ALLOWLIST, not builtins in general. Second instance of this family after the lowercase `case` patterns. I changed my side because a noisy reviewer instrument costs him a round, and the replacement is a better check anyway: `cargo --version` proves the toolchain RUNS rather than that a file sits on PATH. The blind spot goes to him separately rather than being papered over.

HE CLOSED IT, and the class was wider than my two cases: running the family turned up `hash`, `jobs`, `ulimit` and `umask` as well - six builtins - and none could have been filtered out via PATH, because a builtin is not a file, which is precisely why the gap was invisible. The cause he names is the same one behind a stale schema: a list enumerating the members of a known set, maintained by hand beside that set. He replaced the selection with the full bash builtin list, and the decisive calibration is that a genuinely undefined call is STILL caught - all four of my drivers (7, 8, 9, 10) now read clean.

the_build_WRITES_into_the_shared_cargo_r:
His blocking finding, and the fourth instance of one genus on this stream after the index in 3a, the per-worktree FETCH_HEAD in 5 and the reflog in 8. A cold build EXTRACTS `.crate` archives into `~/.cargo/registry/src/`, which is a WRITE into a directory shared by every writer on this machine - I had declared the registry read-only. Measured: the lock names 595 packages while `registry/src` holds fewer unpacked (he counted 478, I count 521 package-version directories at depth 2; the methods differ and the conclusion does not, since both are below 595), so extractions will happen. Now declared as `cache.writes` and in `mutates`.

SECOND HALF, which was absent from my request entirely: `~/.cargo/.package-cache` exists (an empty file dated 2026-04-07) and is cargo's GLOBAL lock on the registry. Two simultaneous builds on this machine serialise on it, and that serialisation is invisible to the gate while the registry is undeclared. Today there is no contention - 0 of 2 leases and `pgrep -x cargo` returns nothing - but the declaration IS the artefact, which is the same argument he used to require the `worktrees/` container from me.
the_twelve_missing_crates_are_NOT_a_pred: His reasoning, kept because it stopped a wrong claim before I could make it. Of the packages not unpacked, 105 have their archive in the cache and 12 have no archive at all - and those 12 are `js-sys`, five `wasm-bindgen*`, `web-sys`, `wasip2`, `wit-bindgen`, `libredox`, `webpki-root-certs` and `skipi-crewing-0.4.139` itself. That is wasm and redox targets plus my own path package. **A Cargo.lock lists the UNION over all targets while a build compiles the graph for ONE**, and cfg conditions are not in the lock - so 'twelve missing therefore the build fails' would be a statement about the wrong population, and it is not derivable from the lock at all. Only cargo knows, which is exactly what `--offline` forces it to say out loud. So this confirms the choice of `--offline` rather than contradicting it.
renew_IS_available_and_drain_is_still_ri:
Correcting my own premise, which he measured as wrong. I implied drain was forced; renew would in fact pass all three of its checks here - `src-tauri/target` is gitignored (`check-ignore` rc 0) and absent, so `git status` does not move and stays the sha of EMPTY output (e3b0c442…); HEAD does not move; and this stage writes none of its own four pins, since it GATES dist/index.html, Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock before and after. His rule 'renew is unavailable to a stage that writes its own pins' simply does not apply to this stage.

Drain remains the choice, on ARITHMETIC rather than on impossibility: renew buys at most one more 300 s window, and a build plausibly running tens of minutes would need 2-8 consecutive renews, each carrying a fresh event, his live inspect and a review MID-BUILD through a human-speed channel. A chain of eight renews is more fragile than one honest drain. The closure sequence is pinned in advance because it cost him four refusals yesterday: `reference --lease-id … --instance …` first, because expiry raises the revision and the certificate held at start stops being current, then `ack-stop --certificate <that file> --evidence <this stage's ACK_STOP> --action-event <its id>`. He verified across all 265 lines that this driver never re-reads the certificate after the start gate, so a revision change cannot affect the run.
a_gate_gap_I_found_in_myself_mirroring_h: After he reported that his `preflight_window` read a pulse from the FUTURE as maximum freshness and advised `grant`, I tested my own window arithmetic with three synthetic certificates rather than assuming mine was sound. An EXPIRED certificate (-623 s remaining) refuses correctly via the floor. But one claiming 86,377 s WOULD HAVE STARTED: the protocol computes expiry as min(now+300, heartbeat+max), so any remainder above 300 s is impossible from a legitimate grant - it means clock skew or a fabricated document - and nothing in my gate looked upward. A bound checked on one side only is half a check. Added WINDOW_CEILING=300 with a named refusal, and re-tested all three: expired refuses on the floor, 257 s starts, 86,377 s refuses above the ceiling. His finding and mine are the same defect pointing in opposite directions, and his positive control with a future timestamp is what made either visible.
the_floor_refused_its_own_stage_and_the_:
The grant came with ~252 s at issuance and my driver refused the start at 200 s against a floor of 240 - the gate did exactly what it was built to do, nothing was written, no ACK_START exists, so the stage never began. But the FLOOR was wrong in kind, and that is measured rather than felt.

ARITHMETIC: expiry 06:01:44Z; his issuance 05:57:31Z (253 s left); certificate written 05:57:37Z (247 s); my launch 05:58:24Z (200 s). Delivery plus one turn of mine consumed 47 s. With a floor of 240 against the 300 s ceiling, the ENTIRE budget for pulse age + his chain + delivery + my turn is 60 s - so 240 was unreachable through a human-speed channel by construction, and no amount of hurrying fixes it.

WHAT THE FLOOR ACTUALLY GUARDED: the precondition block - toolchain check, two rev-parses, porcelain, three digests, disk, canonical count - measures 60 MILLISECONDS. A 240 s floor stood in front of 60 ms of work.

SO THE FLOOR IS NOW 30 s, with a different meaning: it covers the only thing that MUST happen inside the window, namely completing the preconditions and writing ACK_START so the stage legitimately started under the lease. Everything after that is drain territory BY DESIGN, because the build outlasts any lease - which is precisely why a large floor bought nothing while making the stage impossible to begin. The ceiling stays at 300: that one checks a number supplied from outside, and it has a real job.
